summary: Defines an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension for provisioning and managing DNSSEC data for domain names held in a shared registry. It is written in XML and extends the EPP domain name mapping. It is a Proposed Standard and replaced RFC 4310.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells a domain registry how to receive the security details that prove a website name is genuine. A registrar sends either the finished record that the parent zone publishes or the public key itself, and the registry stores and checks it. It replaces an earlier version of the same extension with clearer rules about removing records and about which format to send.

subtitle: How a registrar tells a domain registry which keys sign a name, using an extension to the EPP domain mapping.

tldr.problem: A registry that holds domain names has to be told which keys sign a name, so that the parent zone can publish a record vouching for it. Registrars needed a standard way to hand that information over.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds secDNS elements in XML to the EPP commands for domains. A client sends either Delegation Signer data or the public key itself, and the server stores it, checks it and produces the records the parent zone publishes.
tldr.outcome: This version, secDNS-1.1, replaces secDNS-1.0 from RFC 4310. It makes removal unambiguous, lets one command both add and remove, and adds an interface for servers that accept only key data.

today: RFC 5910 is a Proposed Standard. It replaced RFC 4310, which defined the earlier secDNS-1.0 namespace, and the metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Extension Does
sections.content:
This document is an extension of version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), described in RFC 5730, and of the EPP domain name mapping in RFC 5731. It is specified in XML and XML Schema. Readers are expected to know EPP, the Domain Name System, and the DNS security extensions of RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

The mapping provides a way to provision and manage DNSSEC data for domain names held in a shared central repository. Information exchanged this way can be extracted from the repository and used to publish Delegation Signer (DS) resource records. A DNS server publishes DS information to say that a child zone is digitally signed and that the parent zone recognises the indicated key as a valid zone key for that child zone.

A DS resource record holds four fields: a key tag field, a key algorithm number octet, an octet identifying a digest algorithm, and a digest field. Public key information provided by a client maps to the DNSKEY presentation formats of Section 2.2 of RFC 4034, whose record holds four fields as well: flags, a protocol octet, an algorithm number octet and a public key.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry keeps the list of website names. This document tells registrars how to hand it the security details that prove a name is genuine, so the registry can publish a record vouching for the name to the zone above it.

sections.title: Moving from secDNS-1.0 to secDNS-1.1
sections.content:
The document deprecates secDNS-1.0, so clients and servers need a way to move between the two versions.

If a server announces support for both secDNS-1.0 and secDNS-1.1 in the EPP greeting, clients that support both should prefer secDNS-1.1. A server that is migrating should support both versions for a reasonable migration period.

Which version of the infData element the server returns should depend on the extURI elements the client included in its EPP login command. If urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:secDNS-1.1 was listed, the server returns version 1.1, even if version 1.0 was listed as well. If only version 1.0 was listed, the server returns version 1.0. If neither was listed, the server does not return the infData element at all.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server starts answering in a new format, it keeps answering in the old one for a while. The client says which format it understands when it logs in, and the server replies in that format.

sections.title: The DS Data Interface and the Key Data Interface
sections.content:
A server supports one of two interfaces. In the DS Data Interface, the client is responsible for creating the DS information and passes it for adds and removes, and the server passes DS information back in domain info responses. The server is not obliged to use the key data the client supplies, but the operator may issue out-of-band DNS queries to retrieve the key data from the registered domain's apex in order to evaluate the received DS information. The document recommends that the child zone operator keep that key data online in the DNS tree so the parent zone administrator can validate it, and that the key data have the Secure Entry Point (SEP) bit set.

A dsData element holds a keyTag element, which is an unsignedShort; an alg element; a digestType element; and a digest element, which is a hexBinary. It may also hold an optional keyData child element describing the key used as input in the DS hash calculation, for use in server validation.

In the Key Data Interface, the client passes only key data and the server generates the DS information according to its own policy. A keyData element holds flags, protocol, alg and pubKey, where pubKey is a base64Binary with a minimum length of 1.

Within one command or response the two forms must not be mixed, apart from keyData inside dsData for server validation. A server must use only one form across all create, update and info elements, except during a transition period, during which it may support both, for example on a per-domain basis, so a client can migrate to the target interface. The client replaces the interface by using rem with all set to true to remove all data of the old interface, then add to add data in the new form. A command using an unsupported interface gets EPP error result code 2306.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to hand over the security details. The client can send the finished record that the parent zone publishes, or it can send only the public key and let the registry build the record. A server picks one way and sticks to it.

sections.title: How the EPP Commands Carry the Security Data
sections.content:
The extension adds nothing to the check, delete, renew or transfer commands. It adds elements to info responses and to the create and update commands.

When an info command has been processed successfully, the extension element should contain a secDNS:infData element if the domain object has data associated with this extension and server policy allows. It carries an optional maxSigLife and one or more dsData or keyData elements, but not both. A create command contains a secDNS:create element with an optional maxSigLife and zero or more dsData or keyData elements. If maxSigLife is unsupported, error 2102 must be returned.

An update command contains a secDNS:update element with at least one of add, rem or chg. The order of rem and add is significant: the server must remove the existing elements before adding the new ones. In rem, the all element removes all DS and key data when its value is true. Removing a key can remove more than one DS record, because there can be more than one per key. Removing all DS information can remove the parent's ability to secure the delegation to the child zone.

The update element also takes an optional urgent attribute, whose default value is boolean false, asking the server operator to complete and implement the update with high priority. A server that does not support it returns 2102, and one that supports it but cannot complete the update with high priority returns 2306.
sections.plainLanguage: The same forms you already use to register a name gain a few boxes for the security details. You can add, take away or change them, and take-aways happen before additions.

sections.title: Maximum Signature Lifetime
sections.content:
The optional maxSigLife element is a child's preference for the number of seconds after signature generation when the parent's signature on the DS information provided by the child will expire. It applies to the RRSIG resource record over the DS RRset.

The value must be represented in seconds, using an extended XML Schema int format. The base int format allows negative numbers; this document restricts it further to enforce a minimum value of 1.

If maxSigLife is not provided by the client, or if the server does not support the client-specified value, the default signature expiration policy of the server operator applies. That policy is determined using an out-of-band mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a request for how long the registry's signature on the record should last. It is only a preference: if the registry does not like the number, it applies its own rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mapping extensions described here add no security services beyond those of EPP, the EPP domain name mapping and the protocol layers used by EPP. The security considerations of those specifications apply here as well. The transform operations must be restricted to the sponsoring client, authenticated as described in Sections 2.9.1.1 and 7 of RFC 5730. Any attempt to perform a transform operation by any client other than the sponsoring client must be rejected with an appropriate EPP authorization error.

A trust relationship must exist between the client and the server, and provisioning of public key information must only be done after the identities of both parties have been confirmed using a strong authentication mechanism. A client might act as an agent for a zone administrator who wants delegation information signed and published by the server operator, so man-in-the-middle attacks are possible through direct client activity or inadvertent manipulation of client data.

Acceptance of a false key by a server operator can produce significant operational consequences. The child and parent zones must be consistent to secure the delegation properly; without consistent signatures the delegation will not appear in the secure namespace, which yields untrustworthy query responses. If a key is compromised, a client can remove the compromised information or update the delegation using the urgent attribute. Removing a secure delegation quickly takes two steps: first an urgent update that removes the credentials, then a change of the domain status to either the clientHold or serverHold value. The domain can also be removed from the zone with the delete command, but that is a more drastic step that needs to be considered carefully before use.

Data validity checking and DS record creation at the server require computational resources, so a purposeful or inadvertent denial-of-service attack is possible if a client requests more update operations than the server can process. Server operators should manage command load and processing requirements to reduce that risk. The signature lifetime values from clients are requests that can be rejected, and accepting them blindly can also overload the server, so operators should consider adopting rules that limit the range of acceptable values.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the client that owns the name may change its security details, and the registry must be sure who is asking. Handing over a wrong key can break the name. Checking keys costs the server work, so the server should limit how much work one client can ask for.
